en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sappāṇakavagga 68.
The Training Rule on Ariṭṭha:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a pernicious view had arisen in a monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, as follows:
"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not actually capable of being obstacles for one who indulges in them.
A number of monks heard about this.
“It seems that such an evil view has arisen in the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, named thus:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not actually capable of being obstacles for one who indulges in them.
Then those bhikkhus approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher.
Having approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, they said this to him:
“Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that such an evil view has arisen in you:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them’?”
“Friend, this is how I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: ‘Those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
“Do not say that, friend Ariṭṭha! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One; the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.
In many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstructions, and they are sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them.”
"Sensual pleasures have been described by the Blessed One as having little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is greater still.
Sensual pleasures have been described by the Blessed One as being like a skeleton—having little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is greater still.
Sensual pleasures have been described by the Blessed One as being like a piece of meat... [and so forth].
"Desires have been compared to a grass torch by the Blessed One...
desires have been compared to a pit of glowing coals by the Blessed One...
desires have been compared to a dream by the Blessed One..."
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a sword and a butcher’s block.

“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to spears and spikes… sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to the heads of snakes, full of suffering and despair; herein the danger is even greater.
Even though the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, was addressed thus by those bhikkhus, he stubbornly and obstinately adhered to that evil view and continued to assert it:
“Indeed, friends, this is how I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: ‘Those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
But when those bhikkhus were unable to detach the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly afflicted by vultures, from that evil course of view, they then approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they...
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on that occasion and for that reason, having convened the community of monks, questioned the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly afflicted by vultures:
“Is it true, Ariṭṭha, that such an evil course of view has arisen in you?”
“Do you understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One such that these things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them?
“I do indeed, Bhante, understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: ‘These things called obstructive states by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
“Whose teaching, you foolish man, do you understand as having been taught by me in this way?”
"Is it not so, foolish man, that I have in many ways declared sensual pleasures to be obstructive conditions? They are indeed sufficient to act as obstructions for one who indulges in them.
I have declared that sensual pleasures provide little gratification, but much suffering and much despair; the danger therein is greater still.
I have declared that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton... [and so on].
"Sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a lump of meat...
sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a grass torch...
sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a pit of glowing embers..."
Sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like a dream;
sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like borrowed goods;
sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like the fruit of a tree.

Sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like swords and spears… sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like javelins and spikes… sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like the heads of snakes— full of suffering, full of despair; herein the danger is even greater.
But nevertheless, foolish man, by your own misapprehension you both misrepresent us and ruin yourself, and you generate much demerit.
For that, foolish man, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, monk, should speak thus:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them.’”
That bhikkhu should be addressed by the bhikkhus thus:
“Venerable sir, do not speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak in such a way.
Friend, in many ways the obstructive states have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive, and they are sufficient to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them.”
And if that bhikkhu, being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, should persist as before, that bhikkhu is to be pressed three times by the bhikkhus for the relinquishing of that [position].
If, being pressed up to three times, he should relinquish it, that is good;
if he should not relinquish it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this... "monks" means [as previously defined].
... [as before] ... this is the meaning of "bhikkhu" intended here.
"Should speak thus" means:
"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not actually capable of being obstacles for one who indulges in them."
"Thus, the bhikkhu" refers to that bhikkhu who speaks in such a manner.
"By the bhikkhus" refers to...
Other monks who see or hear of this should say to him:
"Venerable sir, do not speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak in such a way.
Friend, in many ways the obstructive states have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive. And they are indeed sufficient to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them."
He should be told a second time.
He should be told a third time.
If he relinquishes it, that is good.
If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having heard [the charge], if they do not speak, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
That monk should be dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha and addressed thus:
“Do not say this, venerable sir; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus.
In many ways, friend, the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstructive. And they are sufficient to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them.
This should be said a second time as well.
A third time it should be said.
If he relinquishes [the course], that is good.
If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
That monk is to be formally admonished.
And furthermore, monks, he is to be admonished in this way:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
Such an evil view has arisen in the bhikkhu so-and-so:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.’”
Thus he does not relinquish that view.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha formally admonish the monk named so-and-so for the sake of relinquishing that view.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs:
such an evil course of view has arisen in the bhikkhu named so-and-so.

“I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually sufficient to constitute an obstruction for one who indulges in them.
He does not relinquish that view.
The Saṅgha admonishes the monk named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that view.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the monk named so-and-so for the sake of his relinquishing that view, let him be silent;
whichever does not approve, let him speak.
For the second time, I speak this matter... [as before]...
A third time I speak on this matter:
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
Such an evil course of view has arisen in the bhikkhu named so-and-so:
“I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that these things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
He does not relinquish that view.
The Saṅgha admonishes the monk named so-and-so for the sake of relinquishing that view.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the monk named so-and-so for the sake of his relinquishing that view, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has formally admonished the monk named so-and-so for the sake of his relinquishing that view.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
There is an offense of wrong-doing for the motion;
there are offenses of wrong-doing for each of the two formal proclamations.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (kammavācā), there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it is a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma) and one perceives it as such, yet does not desist, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is a legitimate legal act and one is uncertain of it, yet does not desist, there is an offense of expiation.
If one perceives an illegal act as an illegal act and does not relinquish it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one perceives an illegal act as a legal act, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If one is doubtful regarding an illegal act, there is an offense of wrongdoing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and he perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for one who does not formally admonish [the offender].
"For one who relinquishes it," "for one who is insane.
The eighth training rule concerning Arittha is concluded.
